claims.text: Conventional casting typically produces equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state.
The conventionally cast simple solid-solution material has a coarse, homogeneous microstructure.
The conventionally cast material has minimal secondary-phase formation.
The coarse microstructure and scarcity of secondary phases provide limited dislocation pinning.
Grain-boundary and precipitation strengthening are underdeveloped in the cast material.
Underdeveloped grain-boundary and precipitation strengthening causes the material's low hardness and strength.
Powder-metallurgy processing can refine the CoCrFeNiTi microstructure and produce fine grains.
Powder-metallurgy processing may produce nanoscale precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
Fine grains increase strength through Hall-Petch grain-boundary strengthening.
Nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation motion and increase strength through precipitation strengthening.
Powder-metallurgy samples will have higher hardness than composition-matched conventionally cast samples.
Powder-metallurgy samples will have higher strength than composition-matched conventionally cast samples.
Grain size, dislocation density, and secondary-phase distribution govern the barriers to dislocation motion.
The proposed mechanism applies to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi under typical room-temperature hardness and plastic-deformation testing.
The proposed mechanism is limited to samples not subjected to additional heat treatments that induce other microstructural changes.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as a single-phase solid solution, which implies no secondary phase, whereas the other fields describe it as having minimal or limited secondary phases, which permits some secondary-phase material.
